title: All So Simple / Gladys Knight

title: Loop the intro to buy time
hook: Caught with nothing cued? Loop the intro.
voiceover: Caught with nothing cued? Loop the intro. Every controller and CDJ has a loop button, and it's the most underused tool in the booth. When the record you meant to bring in isn't ready, set a 4 or 8-bar loop on the intro of what's playing and let it ride. Nobody in the room hears a loop. They hear a groove holding. It buys you 10, 20, 30 seconds to find the next one, dig your headphones, breathe. I use it every set, especially on requests I didn't plan for. Panic makes trainwrecks. A loop makes time. What's your go-to save when you get caught?

title: Bridging tempos with half/double-time
hook: You can mix 140 into 90. Here's how.
voiceover: You can mix 140 into 90. Here's how. The trick is halftime and double-time. A drill record at 140 feels the same as a boom-bap record at 70 if you hear it in half. A 112 amapiano groove sits close to double a slow soul cut. So instead of forcing a big tempo jump, you let the ear ride the halved or doubled pulse across the blend. Match the kick to the offbeat, not the number on the screen. Once you feel tempo in relationships instead of digits, whole genres open up to each other. What's the widest tempo gap you've bridged clean? Drop the BPMs.
caption: The number on the screen lies to you. 🎚️ A 140 drill record feels identical to a 70 boom-bap record if you hear it in half — that's how you bridge genres that 'shouldn't' mix. Match the kick to the offbeat, not the digits. Once you feel tempo in relationships, everything connects. Widest gap you've bridged clean? Drop the BPMs.

title: Opening slot etiquette
hook: Opening for someone? Don't play their set.
voiceover: Opening for someone? Don't play their set. The biggest mistake young DJs make is treating the warm-up like their prime-time showcase. You get the early slot, the room's half full, and you drop every anthem you own to prove you belong. Now the headliner walks into a crowd that already peaked and heard the hits. Your job in that slot is to build a runway, not land the plane. Play deeper, play groovier, keep it moving up slowly, and leave the big records for the person you're setting up. Do it right and you get booked again. That's the whole game. What's your warm-up philosophy?

title: Check beatgrids before doors
hook: Check your grids before the gig, not during.
voiceover: Check your grids before the gig, not during. Software analyzes your library automatically, and it's mostly right. But mostly isn't good enough in a live room. Older records cut before click tracks drift. Live drummers speed up. Anything with a long intro or a tempo change can grid wrong, and you won't know until a blend falls apart in front of people. So the day before, I run through the new additions, check the downbeat sits on beat one, and fix the ones that lie. 10 minutes at home saves you a trainwreck at midnight. Prep is a skill nobody claps for. How do you prep your library?
caption: Auto-analysis is 'mostly right,' and mostly isn't good enough in a live room. 🎛️ Older records and live-drummer cuts drift; a wrong grid on a long intro won't show up until the blend collapses in front of people. 10 minutes checking downbeats at home saves a midnight trainwreck. Prep is a skill nobody claps for. How do you prep your library?

title: Where amapiano goes in the night
hook: Amapiano too early kills the floor.
voiceover: Amapiano too early kills the floor. It's patient music. Those log drums breathe, the builds are long, the payoff takes bars. Drop it cold into a warm-up and the room reads it as slow. But land it after you've got bodies moving, when people are ready to lock into a groove instead of chasing a drop, and it takes over the night. I bring it in once the floor trusts me, usually mid-set, bridging off a rap acapella or a soulful house record so the shift feels earned. Right record, wrong time still empties a room. When do you drop yours? Tell me the moment.

title: Cue in a loud booth
hook: Loud booth? Cue with one ear.
voiceover: Loud booth? Cue with one ear. When the monitors are pounding and you can barely hear your headphones, don't crank them to dangerous levels chasing the beat. Slide one cup half off, so one ear reads the room and one ear reads the cue. Then stop trying to hear the whole track. Find the kick and the snare, feel the low end in your chest, and match those. You beatmatch with your body as much as your ears in a loud room. Protect your hearing too. It's the only gear you can't replace. How do you cue when the booth is screaming?
caption: Loud booth survival: don't blast your headphones chasing the beat. 🎧 Slide one cup half off — one ear on the room, one on the cue — then stop listening for the whole track and match just the kick and snare. Feel the low end in your chest. You beatmatch with your body too. And protect your ears; it's the one piece of gear you can't replace. How do you cue in a screaming booth?

The drums sit just behind the beat in a way that reportedly broke Miles Davis's brain. He had his band study it. Dilla loved this record. You can hear its drunk, dragging swing all over his work. If You Want Me to Stay lives here too. On the label, look for the original Epic pressing. As a DJ it's a masterclass in feel over precision. What's the record you'd never sell? Tell me below.
caption: Sly & the Family Stone's 'Fresh' (1973) is a producer's holy grail. 🥁 'In Time' drags the drums just behind the beat — Miles Davis reportedly obsessed over it and had his band study it, and you can hear that drunk swing all over Dilla's work. Look for the original Epic pressing. A masterclass in feel over precision. What would you never sell?

title: How to end a set
hook: How you end a set is everything.
voiceover: How you end a set is everything. Anybody can build energy up. The art is landing the plane. Don't just slam the biggest record and walk off. That leaves a room hyped with nowhere to go. I like to peak, hold it, then bring one last record that everybody knows and can sing, something that sends people out into the night on a feeling instead of a drop. Read whether the crowd wants one more climb or a warm goodbye, and give them that. The last record is the one they remember on the walk home. What's your go-to closer? Name it.

title: Coast II Coast at 32
hook: Thirty-two years ago, the Liks went coast to coast.
voiceover: Thirty-two years ago, the Liks went coast to coast. February 28th, 1995. Tha Alkaholiks dropped Coast II Coast on Loud Records. Everyone remembers the party-rap reputation. title: Eye Know / Steely Dan + Otis Redding
hook: Eye Know is Steely Dan and Otis Redding.
voiceover: Eye Know is Steely Dan and Otis Redding. De La Soul, 1989. Prince Paul built that sunny love song on the guitar and vocal from Steely Dan's Peg, and threaded in the whistle from Otis Redding's Dock of the Bay. The crew was barely out of high school when it came out, and Prince Paul was already hearing beats in records nobody else in rap was touching. Two records that share nothing on paper, slick 70s rock and raw Memphis soul, folded into one of the warmest rap songs ever made. Save this and pull both originals. What flip should I break down next?

title: Long Red / Mountain (lineage map)
hook: This 1972 live jam hides in hundreds of records.
voiceover: This 1972 live jam hides in hundreds of records. Mountain played Long Red on stage, and that live recording holds two of the most sampled sounds in hip-hop. A knocking drum break, and Leslie West shouting to the crowd, breathe, louder, yeah. Follow the map. The vocals ran through Nas on It Ain't Hard to Tell, Public Enemy on Louder Than a Bomb, and dozens more. The drums drive Jay-Z's 99 Problems and Tribe's Jazz. One night on stage seeded 50 years of rap. That's the whole point of this series, the record behind the record. Drop the deepest Long Red flip you know, and I'll build the full lineage map from your replies.
caption: Closing the month with the ultimate lineage map: Mountain's live 'Long Red' (1972). 🗺️ Two of the most sampled sounds in hip-hop live here — a knocking drum break and Leslie West's ad-libs ('breathe,' 'louder,' 'yeah'). Nas and Public Enemy took the vocals; Jay-Z's '99 Problems' and Tribe's 'Jazz' took the drums. One stage night, 50 years of rap. Drop the deepest flip and I'll build the full map from your replies.
